before.content_html:
What Is a Business For?

A business is any organisation that produces goods or provides services for customers. Businesses exist to satisfy needs and wants — the things people must have (food, shelter, clothing) and the things people choose to buy (a Greggs sausage roll, a Spotify subscription, a BrewDog beer). Some businesses aim to make a profit for their owners; others, like the British Heart Foundation, exist to serve a cause. In every case the core idea is the same: spot a gap, supply something people will pay for, and do it better or cheaper than the alternatives.

It helps to separate goods from services. Goods are physical — a Tesco ready meal, a pair of Nike trainers. Services are actions performed for customers — a Deliveroo drop-off, a Vets4Pets consultation. Most modern businesses sell a blend of both: a Wetherspoons pub sells burgers (goods) alongside table service and an atmosphere (service).

Key Fact

Businesses supply goods and services to meet needs (essentials) and wants (preferences). The more clearly a business identifies a gap between what customers need or want and what is currently available, the stronger its chance of survival.

The Four Factors of Production

To produce anything, a business combines four factors of production. Land covers all natural resources — the site of a Greggs bakery, the wheat in its flour, the water in its drinks. Labour is the human effort involved, from shop floor staff to the head baker. Capital means the man-made resources used to produce other goods — ovens, delivery vans, tills. Enterprise is the risk-taking skill that pulls the other three together — the entrepreneur who decides to open a branch in a new town and raises the money to do it.

Opportunity Cost

Opportunity cost is the value of what you give up whenever you make a decision. If Innocent Drinks spends £500,000 on a new factory oven, that same £500,000 cannot be spent on a marketing campaign. The opportunity cost of the oven is the marketing that was sacrificed. Every business decision has one — even your own time, because revising one subject means not revising another.

The Three Sectors

UK businesses sit in one of three sectors. The primary sector extracts raw materials — think farming, fishing, mining. The secondary sector turns those materials into finished products — a Jaguar Land Rover factory assembling cars. The tertiary sector provides services — Lloyds Bank, Vodafone, the NHS. Most jobs in the UK are in the tertiary sector because our economy is service-led.

A hundred years ago, manufacturing dominated the UK economy. Today, cheaper labour abroad has pulled most factory work overseas, while digital technology has created whole new tertiary businesses — Deliveroo, Monzo, Bumble. Understanding the shift matters because where a business sits affects how it competes: a primary-sector dairy farmer faces supermarket price pressure, while a tertiary tech firm competes on ideas and speed.

What Makes an Entrepreneur?

An entrepreneur is the person who takes the financial risk of starting a business. They spot a gap in the market, gather the factors of production and take the personal hit if the idea fails. Characteristics that recur in successful entrepreneurs include being hard working, innovative, well organised and willing to take a calculated risk. James Watt-Smith (Gousto), Sophie Trelawney (Trinny London) and James Watt (BrewDog) all left comfortable jobs because they backed their idea.

Their motives vary. Many want to be their own boss and control their own hours. Others are chasing a passion — turning a hobby into a living. Some spot a gap in the market that no-one else has filled. Some are simply dissatisfied with their current job and want to earn more. Most combine several of these reasons.

Key Fact

Every business combines land, labour, capital and enterprise. Remove any one and production stops — a bakery without ovens (capital) or without bakers (labour) cannot make bread, no matter how good the recipe.

The Dynamic Business Environment

Businesses face a constantly shifting environment. Technology creates new opportunities (contactless payments) and kills old ones (HMV lost out to streaming). The economy expands and contracts — rising interest rates squeezed customer spending in 2023. Legislation changes what firms can do, from minimum wage rises to plastic-bag charges. Environmental expectations now push businesses to cut waste and emissions. Firms that adapt quickly survive; those that don’t, like Thomas Cook or Debenhams, disappear.

When Greggs opened its first evening-only food-to-go site, the opportunity cost was the revenue from not opening a standard daytime bakery on that site. When an entrepreneur takes a redundancy payout and invests it in stock rather than putting it in a savings account, the opportunity cost is the interest they would have earned. Strong answers in this topic always name the specific alternative that was given up — ‘the money could have been used for X’ — rather than saying ‘there was an opportunity cost’.

Why Legal Structure Matters

Before a business trades, its owners have to decide what kind of organisation it will be. The legal structure chosen affects how much control the owners keep, how profits are shared, where the business can raise money, and crucially, what happens if things go wrong. A self-employed dog walker and Tesco PLC are both businesses, but they operate under very different rules. Choosing the wrong structure can cripple a good idea — so this decision is one of the first serious tests for any entrepreneur.

Sole Traders

A sole trader is a business with one owner. Think of a local plumber, a market-stall holder or a personal trainer. Setting up is simple: register with HMRC and start trading. The owner keeps all the profit and makes every decision. The downside is the same detail that makes it attractive — the owner is the business in the eyes of the law. They face unlimited liability, meaning if the business owes money it cannot repay, creditors can come after the owner’s house, car and savings.

Key Fact

Sole traders keep all the profit and have full control, but they have unlimited liability and limited ways to raise finance. Most UK businesses are sole traders — simple to set up, but risky if the business fails.

Partnerships

A partnership has between 2 and 20 owners who share the workload, combine their skills and pool capital. A high-street solicitor, a local accountancy firm and most GP surgeries run as partnerships. Decisions are shared, profits are split according to a partnership agreement, and more finance can be raised than by one individual. The drawback is that partners still have unlimited liability — and one partner’s mistake can land the others with the bill. Disagreements between partners also slow decisions.

Private Limited Companies (Ltd)

A private limited company (Ltd) is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders. Shares can be sold to family, friends or invited investors but not to the general public. Most UK companies with ‘Ltd’ at the end — Greggs was one before it floated, Dyson still is — fall into this category. The crucial advantage is limited liability. If the company goes bust, shareholders can only lose the money they put in; their personal assets are safe. In return, Ltds must register at Companies House and publish annual accounts.

Public Limited Companies (Plc)

A public limited company (Plc) can sell shares to the general public through the stock exchange. Tesco PLC, BT Group PLC and JD Sports Fashion PLC are household examples. Going public opens up huge sources of finance — millions of pounds can be raised in a single share issue — and raises brand profile. The catch: ownership is diluted, takeovers become possible, and every result is scrutinised by shareholders and the press. Plcs also face strict reporting and must publish detailed annual reports.

Both Ltds and Plcs have limited liability and are separate legal entities. The key difference is how they raise money. An Ltd can only sell shares to people it invites; a Plc can sell to anyone through the London Stock Exchange. That changes the scale of finance available — and the amount of outside control the owners must accept. When Aston Martin floated as a Plc in 2018, the founders accepted public scrutiny of every quarterly result in return for the cash to expand globally.

The decision to move from Ltd to Plc is called a flotation or Initial Public Offering (IPO). Many UK family businesses stay as Ltds precisely because they want to keep control inside the family. Going public is almost impossible to undo cheaply.

Not-for-Profit Organisations

Some organisations exist to serve a social or charitable purpose rather than to make profit for owners. Charities like Oxfam and the British Heart Foundation are not-for-profit organisations. They still have to cover costs, pay staff and manage cash — but any surplus is reinvested into the cause rather than paid out to shareholders. Social enterprises like The Big Issue operate the same way: they sell a product to fund a mission.

Key Fact

Limited liability protects the owners’ personal assets — it does not protect the business itself. A company can still go bust; limited liability simply caps how much each shareholder can personally lose at the amount they invested.

A lone builder just starting out will usually begin as a sole trader — cheap, simple, no reporting. Two dental graduates opening a practice together are suited to a partnership — shared skills, shared finance. A growing family catering business taking on larger contracts will often become a private limited company to protect the owners’ homes from supplier claims. A national retailer needing hundreds of millions to open stores will eventually list as a Plc. The right structure depends on the size of the business, the risk it faces, and how much outside finance it needs.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following types of business has unlimited liability?
A) Public limited company (Plc)
B) Private limited company (Ltd)
C) Sole trader
D) Registered charity
practice_questions.marks:
C) Sole trader [1 mark]
Plcs and Ltds have limited liability; registered charities operate under separate charity law.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'limited liability'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: shareholders can only lose a limited amount / protects the owners.
2 marks: shareholders can only lose the amount they invested in the company — their personal assets are protected if the company goes bust. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage for a growing family bakery of becoming a private limited company rather than remaining a sole trader.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an advantage (limited liability, easier to raise finance from invited shareholders, separate legal identity, continuity if an owner leaves).
2 marks: a 'because' clause explains it.
3 marks: links to the specific bakery context.
Indicative answer: 'Becoming an Ltd gives the owners limited liability (1), meaning if the bakery failed they would only lose the money they invested, not their family home (2). This matters as the bakery takes on bigger supplier contracts where the financial risk is higher (3).' [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how unlimited liability could affect the decisions made by the owner of a small mobile car-wash business.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning that trace unlimited liability → owner decision → business consequence, applied to the car-wash context.
Secure: Two chains, one fully developed, relevant to the context.
Developing: Identifies effects with partial development, limited application.
Emerging: Defines unlimited liability without linking it to decisions.
Indicative chains: (1) avoids borrowing large sums → can't afford a second van → growth slower than rivals; (2) takes out personal insurance to protect house → extra cost eats into profit → may raise prices; (3) avoids hiring staff → keeps business small → limits revenue. Students may also pick one factor and develop it in depth, as the 2026 assessment approach allows. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Two friends are launching an online fashion brand. Justify whether they should begin as a partnership or as a private limited company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the alternative, applied to an online fashion context with reference to limited liability and finance needs.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists features of both without a supported recommendation.
Indicative content for Partnership: cheap to set up, simple, shared decisions, profits split as agreed; unlimited liability is a concern because fashion stock can go out of date fast. For Ltd: limited liability protects them if unsold stock creates debt; can sell shares to family/friends for launch capital; more admin and filing costs. A strong answer lands on limited liability as the critical factor for a stock-heavy online business. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Every growing business should aim to become a public limited company.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: huge access to finance through share issues (e.g. JD Sports expansion); limited liability; raised brand profile; separate legal identity gives stability; ability to attract top management via share options.
Arguments to challenge: loss of control as ownership diluted across thousands of shareholders; vulnerability to hostile takeovers; pressure to deliver short-term profits for the stock market; costly reporting and compliance; many successful UK businesses (Dyson, Specsavers) stay as Ltds deliberately; a small local cafe has no need for Plc-scale finance.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to real examples, and a judgement that introduces a new weighting (e.g. 'depends on the size and finance needs of the business').
Secure: Balanced argument with development on both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side with limited development.
Emerging: One-sided list with no evaluation. [12 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which feature is shared by private limited companies (Ltd) and public limited companies (Plc) but NOT by sole traders?
options: All profits go to one person
Shares are sold on the stock exchange

knowledge_checks.q: What is the maximum number of partners in a traditional partnership?
A _____ company can sell its shares on the stock exchange to any member of the public.
A charity or social enterprise reinvests its surplus rather than paying it to shareholders — it is a _____ organisation.
Match each legal structure to a typical example:
right: Dyson, owned by the Dyson family
Tesco, with shares on the London Stock Exchange

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the most likely main objective for a business in its first year of trading?
A) Maximising shareholder value
B) International expansion
C) Survival
D) Achieving a 20% market share
practice_questions.marks:
C) Survival [1 mark]
In year one, covering costs and building a customer base matters more than large-scale targets.

practice_questions.text: Give two objectives that a public limited company (Plc) such as JD Sports might set itself.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid objective (max 2): profit maximisation, growth (domestic or international), market share, customer satisfaction, social/ethical objectives (e.g. sustainability), shareholder value. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business had total sales of £1,200,000. The total size of the market was £20,000,000. Calculate the business's market share. Give your answer as a percentage.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: 1,200,000 ÷ 20,000,000 = 0.06 (1 mark for correct division).
Convert to percentage: 0.06 × 100 = 6 (1 mark).
Final answer with unit: 6% (1 mark).
Method marks awarded even if the final figure is wrong, provided the working is shown. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a business's objectives might change as it grows from a single-site start-up into a national chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning tracing how objectives shift, with named stages (e.g. survival → profit maximisation → growth → shareholder value/ethical) and clear cause-and-effect.
Secure: Two chains, at least one developed, relevant to a named business or realistic scenario.
Developing: Lists changes with limited explanation.
Emerging: States objectives without explaining the shift.
Indicative chains: (1) early on survival dominates because costs outstrip revenue → later, once cash flow stabilises, profit maximisation becomes possible → at national scale, growth and shareholder value take over because the business must justify itself to investors. (2) ethical/social objectives often emerge later because small firms cannot afford the extra cost → as scale brings profit, the business can invest in sustainability which also protects its brand. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A growing bakery chain is choosing between (A) aggressive growth — opening 30 new stores in two years — or (B) focusing on customer satisfaction and slow, steady expansion. Justify which objective you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to a bakery chain, with explicit reference to risks and context (finance, competition, customer loyalty).
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting of the alternative.
Emerging: Lists advantages and disadvantages without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A: rapid market share gain locks competitors out; economies of scale drive down unit costs; but diseconomies of scale and cash-flow strain are real risks (see Patisserie Valerie collapse). For B: protects brand reputation, builds repeat custom, lower cash-flow risk; but rivals may grab market share first. Strong answers name the deciding factor (e.g. strength of competition, availability of finance) rather than defaulting to safety. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The only objective that really matters for a business is maximising profit.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments for and against the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: profit funds investment and survival; without it a business eventually closes; shareholders expect a return; profit is the most objective measure of performance.
Arguments to challenge: a short-term profit focus can damage long-term performance (e.g. cutting quality reduces repeat custom); not-for-profits like Oxfam succeed without profit; ethical objectives build brand loyalty (Patagonia, Tony's Chocolonely); customer satisfaction often precedes profit; stakeholder conflict is worsened by pure profit focus; staff motivation can suffer.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'profit matters most in the short term for survival, but ethical and customer objectives protect profit in the long term').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument or generic list. [12 marks]

before.content_html:
Who Are Stakeholders?

A stakeholder is anyone who is affected by or has an interest in what a business does. When a new Greggs opens in a town, the impact spreads far wider than the bakery itself — owners expect profit, staff gain jobs, customers get sausage rolls, rival coffee shops lose trade, suppliers win a new contract, and the local community gets a bit more footfall. Each of these groups has a different ‘stake’ in the decision. Understanding stakeholders matters because every big business choice helps some and hurts others — and those who are hurt will push back.

The Five Main Stakeholder Groups

The specification focuses on five groups. Owners (sole traders, partners or shareholders) invest their money and time. They want profits, dividends and a rising share value. Employees depend on the business for their pay and security. Customers want good value products and reliable service. Suppliers want to be paid on time and receive repeat orders. The local community wants jobs and investment, but objects to noise, pollution or traffic.

Key Fact

The five main stakeholder groups are owners, employees, customers, suppliers and the local community. Each has different, often competing, objectives — the business must balance them to succeed.

What Each Stakeholder Wants

Owners want dividends and a rising share price. Employees want high wages, job security, safe working conditions and the chance to develop. Customers want quality products at fair prices, honest advertising and good post-sales service. Suppliers want prompt payment and long-term contracts so they can plan their own business. The local community wants employment opportunities and minimal environmental impact — if Amazon opens a new warehouse, locals want the jobs but not the lorries clogging the road at 4am.

Some revision texts add the government (which wants tax revenue and employment) and pressure groups (which want specific changes, such as plastic-free packaging). The assessed five remain the core.

The Impact of Business Activity on Stakeholders

Every business decision radiates out to different stakeholders. When Morrisons cuts 150 middle-management jobs, shareholders may cheer the cost savings while the affected employees lose their income and morale drops across the remaining workforce. When a new Aldi opens in a town, customers gain lower prices, but independent grocers nearby may lose enough trade to close. When Tesla opens a Gigafactory, the local community gets thousands of jobs, but also extra traffic and pressure on local housing. Even an apparently positive decision — raising staff wages, for example — can be divisive: employees welcome the rise, owners see profits dip, and customers face higher prices as costs are passed on. Good managers ask, before every major choice, ‘who benefits, who pays, and how loudly will the losers object?’ A decision that ignores this question rarely survives contact with reality.

Imagine a delivery firm decides to switch to 24-hour operations. Owners benefit — higher revenue and better use of vans. Customers benefit — overnight deliveries. Employees split: some welcome the night-shift premium, others hate the hours. Suppliers near the depot must also work later. The local community loses — sleep-disturbing lorry noise at 3am. This is stakeholder conflict: one decision, multiple opposing reactions. The business cannot please everyone, so it must judge which group matters most to its success.

How Stakeholders Influence Businesses

Stakeholders have levers they can pull. Owners and shareholders can vote at annual general meetings, replace directors or refuse further investment. Employees can work harder, strike, quit, or go slow — poor treatment kills productivity. Customers vote with their wallets: when Boohoo was linked to underpaid factory workers in Leicester, sales fell and the share price halved. Suppliers can demand upfront payment or refuse to extend credit when a firm becomes risky. The local community can block planning applications or run a campaign through the local media.

Different stakeholders carry different weight. A Tesco Plc decision is shaped heavily by big shareholders, while a village cafe lives or dies on the goodwill of its local community. This is why good 9-mark and 12-mark answers always ask: which stakeholder has the most influence in this context? The answer shifts over time too: a start-up depends heavily on its first customers and early investors; a mature Plc answers to thousands of shareholders and City analysts. The shift from private to public ownership often means managers now spend more time managing investor expectations than they do serving customers.

Key Fact

Stakeholder objectives often conflict: owners want dividends, employees want higher pay, customers want lower prices, and the local community wants minimal disruption. A business cannot maximise all at once — managing the trade-offs is a core leadership skill.

Businesses resolve conflicts through trade-offs and communication. A factory can invest in quieter machinery to reduce community complaints while preserving production. A supermarket can introduce self-checkouts (cuts costs, helps shareholders) but redeploy staff into personal shopping roles rather than making them redundant. Clear communication — explaining a decision honestly — often softens the blow even when the decision itself is unpopular. The businesses that survive conflict best are those that treat stakeholders as partners rather than obstacles.
before.exam_tip_html: For ‘Analyse’ questions on stakeholders, pick one group and develop the chain of reasoning rather than listing all five superficially. A good answer reads ‘Employees are stakeholders because their pay depends on the business — if the business cuts jobs, employees lose income, which reduces their spending power and damages staff morale among those who remain.’ On evaluation questions about whose interests come first, avoid saying ‘the owners always matter most’ — context decides. For a co-operative like John Lewis, employees are the owners.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a stakeholder group that would MOST directly oppose a decision to open a 24-hour warehouse next to a housing estate?
A) Shareholders
B) Customers
C) The local community
D) Suppliers
practice_questions.marks:
C) The local community [1 mark]
Noise, traffic and pollution at night directly affect residents living nearby.

practice_questions.text: Give two objectives that suppliers of a business usually have.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid objective (max 2): prompt payment, repeat orders, long-term contracts, fair prices, clear communication about changing demand. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why employees could be considered the most important stakeholder group for a small family restaurant.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (skilled staff affect quality; staff represent the brand to customers; low turnover saves recruitment costs; staff motivation drives customer service).
2 marks: a 'because' clause explains the reason.
3 marks: links to the specific family restaurant context.
Indicative answer: 'Employees directly shape the customer experience (1) because diners remember the quality of service, food presentation and friendliness more than the restaurant's advertising (2), so for a family restaurant relying on repeat custom, staff are the single biggest driver of success (3).' [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a decision by a large supermarket to switch to self-service checkouts could affect two of its stakeholder groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two groups chosen, each developed into a full chain of reasoning (stakeholder → consequence → business impact), with clear cause-effect logic.
Secure: Two groups with at least one fully developed chain.
Developing: Two groups named with partial development.
Emerging: Lists groups without explaining impact.
Indicative chains: (1) Employees — fewer cashiers needed → redundancies or redeployment → lower morale, possible strike action → disruption to store operations. (2) Customers — faster queues for small baskets → convenience for regulars, but older or less digitally confident customers feel excluded → lost sales to rival supermarkets with staffed tills. (3) Shareholders — lower wage bill → higher profit margins → rising dividend. Students may develop one factor in depth per the 2026 approach. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A clothing retailer is deciding whether to (A) raise prices to fund a 10% pay rise for warehouse staff or (B) keep prices flat and pay a larger dividend to shareholders. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to a retailer with explicit reference to stakeholder impact and brand reputation.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists impacts without a supported recommendation.
Indicative content for A: improves staff retention and productivity, protects brand reputation after fast-fashion pay scandals (e.g. Boohoo), appeals to ethical consumers; but risks losing price-sensitive customers in a tough market. For B: rewards owners, signals a strong financial performance to investors, supports share price; but risks strike action, media backlash and reputational damage. A strong answer names whether long-term brand protection or short-term shareholder return should drive the decision. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Shareholders should always come first when a business makes a decision.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: shareholders own the business and fund its operations; without their capital the business could not exist; dividends and share price are the reward for risk; Plcs are legally answerable to shareholders; aligned incentives drive efficiency.
Arguments to challenge: ignoring staff causes strikes, recruitment costs and reputational damage (e.g. Amazon warehouse disputes); unhappy customers switch to rivals; supplier relationships break down; community opposition can block planning; ethical brands (Patagonia, Tony's Chocolonely) thrive precisely by putting people or planet before pure shareholder returns; long-term shareholder value is damaged by short-term-only thinking.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'depends on the ownership structure and time horizon').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side with limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument without evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which location factor is MOST important for a new independent coffee shop opening in a town centre?
A) Proximity to raw materials
B) Proximity to the market (customers)
C) Proximity to government offices
D) Proximity to a university library
practice_questions.marks:
B) Proximity to the market (customers) [1 mark]
A coffee shop depends on passing foot traffic — without customers within walking distance it will fail regardless of other factors.

practice_questions.text: Give two costs that are likely to differ between locating a warehouse in central London and locating one in Doncaster.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid difference (max 2): rent / business rates, wages (higher in London), transport / delivery costs to London markets, utilities, congestion charges. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A retailer pays £480,000 in annual rent at its current site. A new site costs £300,000 per year. Calculate the percentage saving the retailer would make on rent by moving. Give your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: saving = £480,000 − £300,000 = £180,000 (1 mark).
Percentage saving = 180,000 ÷ 480,000 × 100 (1 mark for correct method).
= 37.5% (1 mark for final answer with unit).
Method marks awarded for showing working even if final number is slightly off. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the factors a fish and chip restaurant might consider when choosing where to locate in a small UK seaside town.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more factors developed with clear chains of reasoning tying the factor to a specific effect on the restaurant (e.g. proximity to market → near the seafront car park and promenade → high summer footfall → higher revenue). Draws on 2026 approach allowing multiple factors with developed reasoning.
Secure: Two factors explained with relevant cause-and-effect links, applied to a seaside context.
Developing: Lists factors with partial explanation.
Emerging: Names factors without explaining their impact.
Indicative content: proximity to market (seafront footfall), raw materials (local fish supplies, cost of transport if inland), labour (seasonal staff availability), competition (too close to rivals = split trade), costs (beachfront rent vs back-street rent). A developed answer identifies the trade-off: high seafront rent vs high footfall. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: An online clothing start-up is choosing between (A) leasing a warehouse unit in central Manchester close to its staff or (B) leasing a larger unit 40 miles outside Manchester near the M6 motorway. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to an online clothing retailer with reference to specific factors (transport, labour, rent, delivery speed).
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited evaluation.
Emerging: Lists pros and cons without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A: easier to attract and retain staff, shorter commute = better morale, proximity to city suppliers and returns processing; higher rent and business rates, congestion slows delivery vans. For B: cheaper rent means more space for stock, direct motorway access speeds next-day delivery, easier to scale; but recruiting and retaining staff harder, commute costs may deter applicants. A strong answer names the deciding factor — delivery speed or staff retention — and links it back to the start-up's growth stage. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Cost is always the most important factor when choosing a business location.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments for and against the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: cost directly affects profit margins and break-even; high rent or wages can sink a small business (e.g. high-street closures after rent rises); cheap locations free up cash for investment; government grants and cheap regions (e.g. Enterprise Zones) deliberately use cost to attract firms.
Arguments to challenge: a cheap site with no customers has no revenue; luxury brands need prestige addresses (Bond Street jewellers); manufacturers must be near raw materials; service businesses need footfall; skilled labour may only exist in expensive regions (tech in Cambridge, finance in London); long-term brand damage from a poor address can cost more than the rent saved.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to real businesses, and a judgement that introduces a new weighting (e.g. 'cost matters most for firms competing on low prices; prestige or access matters most for firms competing on experience').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument without evaluation. [12 marks]

before.content_html:
Why Plan?

A business plan is a written document that sets out what a business will do, who its customers are, and how it expects to make money. It forces entrepreneurs to think before they spend — to answer hard questions about whether an idea actually makes financial sense. Banks, investors and landlords want to see a plan before they commit. Even an established firm updates its plan when it launches a new product. The discipline of writing the plan often matters more than the document itself: it exposes flawed assumptions early, while they are cheap to fix.

What Goes in a Plan

Typical sections include the business idea and aims, the target market, a marketing plan, an operations plan, details of management and staff, and financial forecasts — including costs, revenue and a cash-flow forecast. Plans aren’t just about raising finance. They help set objectives, guide decisions and track progress. The drawbacks: plans take time to write, are based on predictions that may be wrong, and can give false confidence if markets move unexpectedly (as many did during Covid).

Key Fact

Business plans help secure finance, set objectives, guide decisions and reduce risk — but they cost time to write, rely on forecasts that can go wrong, and risk going out of date quickly. Note you are not expected to write a plan in the exam — only to explain its purpose.

Financial Terms You Must Know

Fixed costs do not change when output changes. Rent on a bakery unit is the same whether you bake 100 loaves or 1,000. Variable costs change with output — double the loaves and you double the flour. Total costs equal fixed plus variable costs. Revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. Profit is revenue minus total costs; if costs exceed revenue, the business makes a loss.

A quick worked example: a bakery sells 1,000 loaves at £2 each. Revenue = £2,000. Variable costs are 60p per loaf (= £600). Fixed costs are £900 per month. Total costs = £1,500. Profit = £500. Increase output to 1,500 loaves and variable costs rise to £900, but fixed costs stay at £900 — spreading the fixed cost over more loaves lowers the average cost per loaf.

Methods of Growth

Once a business is stable, owners often want to grow. There are two broad paths. Organic growth means growing under your own steam — opening new stores, expanding online, outsourcing non-core tasks, or signing up franchisees. Greggs has grown organically from a single Newcastle shop to over 2,500 UK sites. External growth means combining with another business — a merger joins two firms as equals, while a takeover sees one firm buy another outright. Morrisons’ 2005 takeover of Safeway instantly doubled its store network.

Franchising is a fast route to organic growth: the franchisor (e.g. Subway) lets a franchisee open a branded outlet in return for set-up fees and a share of revenue. The franchisee puts in the capital, the franchisor keeps tight control over the brand. Many McDonald’s in the UK are franchised. E-commerce has opened up another route — ASOS grew globally without opening any shops at all, using the internet to reach customers in more than 200 countries.

Organic growth is slower but cheaper and safer — the owners know each new shop because they opened it. External growth is faster but riskier: it is easy to overpay for a rival, and merging two different cultures often fails (the AOL–Time Warner merger is the classic cautionary tale). External growth can also trigger redundancies as duplicate roles are cut, damaging staff morale across both firms.

Economies of Scale

Economies of scale happen when growing output reduces the average cost per unit. Two main types appear in the specification. Purchasing economies — a large supermarket like Tesco buys milk in such huge volumes that suppliers give it a discount. Technical economies — a large factory can afford specialist machinery that a small workshop cannot. Both push down the average cost of making each product, which allows the business to cut prices, raise profit margins, or invest the difference back into the firm.

Diseconomies of Scale

Diseconomies of scale happen when growing further starts to raise average costs rather than lower them. The usual causes: poor communication (head office and shop floor lose touch), coordination issues (too many layers of management, slow decisions) and reduced staff motivation (workers feel like a number in a huge workforce). Many retailers — including parts of Marks & Spencer in the 2010s — hit diseconomies once they expanded too quickly. A strong answer recognises that growth and efficiency are not automatic: scale can hurt as well as help.

Key Fact

Average unit cost = total costs ÷ units produced. Economies of scale push this figure down; diseconomies push it up. Growth is only valuable if the average unit cost keeps falling — otherwise the extra sales cost too much to make.

A small bakery has total costs of £1,500 and produces 1,000 loaves. Average unit cost = 1,500 ÷ 1,000 = £1.50 per loaf. If output rises to 2,000 loaves and total costs rise only to £2,400 (thanks to bulk flour discounts), average unit cost falls to £2,400 ÷ 2,000 = £1.20 per loaf. That 30p saving per loaf is the economy of scale. If the bakery grows further and the owner can no longer oversee quality, wastage rises, total costs climb to £4,500 for 3,000 loaves, and average unit cost rises to £1.50 again — a diseconomy of scale.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a fixed cost for a small bakery?
A) The flour used to make bread
B) The electricity used per loaf baked
C) The monthly rent on the shop unit
D) The packaging for each loaf
practice_questions.marks:
C) The monthly rent on the shop unit [1 mark]
Rent does not change with the number of loaves produced; flour, electricity per loaf and packaging all vary with output.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: reduction in average cost as output grows / cost advantages of being larger.
2 marks: the cost advantages a business gains as it grows, reducing the average cost per unit — e.g. bulk-buying discounts or specialist machinery. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business has fixed costs of £4,000 and variable costs of £3 per unit. If it produces 2,000 units, calculate the average unit cost. Give your answer in £ to two decimal places.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: variable cost total = 2,000 × £3 = £6,000 (1 mark).
Total cost = £4,000 + £6,000 = £10,000 (1 mark).
Average unit cost = £10,000 ÷ 2,000 = £5.00 (1 mark for final answer with unit).
Method marks awarded for showing working even if final number is wrong. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how economies of scale could benefit a growing supermarket chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning linking an economy of scale to a specific business benefit (e.g. purchasing → bulk discounts from milk suppliers → lower price for customers → market share grows). Applied to a supermarket chain.
Secure: Two economies identified and explained with at least one full chain.
Developing: Lists economies of scale with partial explanation.
Emerging: States economies without explaining their effects.
Indicative chains: (1) purchasing economies — bulk buying → lower per-unit input costs → higher margin or lower price → competitive advantage over smaller rivals. (2) Technical economies — specialist distribution centres and automated warehousing → lower cost per delivery → efficiency improvements. (3) Marketing economies — national advertising campaigns spread across more stores → cost per store falls. May develop one in depth. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A family-owned coffee chain with 12 shops is choosing between (A) expanding organically by opening new branches one at a time, or (B) buying a struggling rival chain of 15 branches in one takeover. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to the coffee chain with explicit reference to financing, risk, culture and economies of scale.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists features of both without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A (organic): slower but lower risk, retains family control, each new branch learnt from carefully, cash flow manageable; but rivals may expand faster. For B (takeover): instant scale brings purchasing economies, removes a competitor, but needs a large lump sum of finance, rival sites may be loss-making, staff culture clashes, risk of diseconomies of scale. Strong answers identify the deciding factor — available finance, speed of the market, or cultural fit. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'A business should always try to grow as large as possible.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: economies of scale reduce average unit cost and raise profit margins; bigger firms have more bargaining power with suppliers; larger firms attract better staff and cheaper finance; market share protects against competition; brand recognition drives customer loyalty.
Arguments against: diseconomies of scale raise average unit cost when firms overstretch (Patisserie Valerie, parts of M&S); communication and motivation suffer in large firms; takeovers often destroy value (AOL–Time Warner); small firms can compete on quality and personal service (independent cafes, boutique brands); growth requires finance that may dilute owner control; many family firms deliberately stay small to protect culture.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'growth is valuable only while average unit costs keep falling and management can still communicate clearly').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument or list without evaluation. [12 marks]
